To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interaction between threat and self-efficacy is significant (d = 1.03), and the interaction between threat, efficacy and outcome is also significant (d =.71).
threat only has an effect under high levels of efficacy (d =.31) and efficacy only has an effect when threat levels are high (d =.71).
the effect of threat is moderated by efficacy, and that the effectiveness of fear appeals can be predicted with high accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effectiveness of threatening messages in changing behaviour.
the effectiveness of threatening communications.
the effects of fear appeals in persuasive health communication and the role of threat in fear appeal effectiveness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
threat only works when people believe they have the means to deal with the threat.
fear appeal theory is valid, but only under conditions of high perceived self-efficacy.
fear appeal theory is valid, and threatening communication can be effective, but only when efficacy is enhanced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the threat of negative consequences is only effective when the efficacy of the recommended behaviour is enhanced.
threatening communication can only have an effect when the recipient believes that he/she is capable of coping with the threat.
the meta-analysis shows that fear appeals are effective when they are used to increase efficacy, but that fear appeals do not increase efficacy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the dynamics of fear appeal theory should be considered as a function of the efficacy of the advocated behaviour.
the effectiveness of threatening appeals is highly dependent on the efficacy of the intervention.
threatening communication can be effective, but only under certain circumstances.
